import re

def parse_duration(s: str) -> int:
    if not s or not isinstance(s, str):
        raise ValueError(f"Invalid duration string: {s!r}")
    
    pattern = r'^(?:(\d+)h)?(?:(\d+)m)?(?:(\d+)s)?$'
    match = re.match(pattern, s)
    
    if not match or not any(match.groups()):
        raise ValueError(f"Invalid duration string: {s!r}")
    
    hours = int(match.group(1)) if match.group(1) is not None else 0
    minutes = int(match.group(2)) if match.group(2) is not None else 0
    seconds = int(match.group(3)) if match.group(3) is not None else 0
    
    return hours * 3600 + minutes * 60 + seconds

Eventual consistency means that when a customer makes a change, every part of the system may not reflect that change immediately, but if no new changes are made, all parts will converge to the same correct state after a short period of time. In practice, this can mean a user updates a setting, uploads a file, or changes an order status, and for a few seconds—or in some systems, longer—another screen, report, search result, or user may still see the old value. The key customer promise should not be “everyone sees every change instantly,” unless the product is specifically designed for that; instead, promise something like “changes are saved immediately and may take up to X seconds/minutes to appear everywhere,” and be clear about which actions are safe during that window. For customer-critical workflows like payments, inventory, permissions, or compliance records, you may need stronger guarantees or visible safeguards, because “eventually correct” can still feel broken if users make decisions based on stale information.

Eventual consistency means that when a customer makes a change to their data, that change is accepted right away and the system feels fast and reliable, but it may take a few seconds or longer before every part of the system has caught up and shows exactly the same value to everyone. In practice this lets you promise customers that their updates will never be lost and the service will stay available even if some servers or regions have problems, while also warning them that for a short time they or their teammates might briefly see slightly older information. The key question to ask when deciding what to promise is whether the feature can tolerate that brief window of possible mismatch; if a user is updating a shared document or a shopping cart, a short delay is usually acceptable and you can set expectations like “changes appear within a few seconds,” but if the same user is checking a bank balance or real-time inventory that must never appear wrong, you may need to invest in stronger guarantees or different user-facing language so you don’t over-promise perfect immediacy.

When you save something in our system — say, updating your profile picture — that change gets written to one server and then quietly copied to several others in the background, which usually takes anywhere from a fraction of a second to a few seconds. During that tiny window, two different users (or even the same user on two different devices) might briefly see different versions of the data, like one person still seeing the old photo while another sees the new one. Eventually, all the servers catch up and everyone sees the same thing — hence "eventual consistency." For customers, this means you should avoid promising that a change will be instantly visible everywhere the moment it's saved; instead, promise that changes will be reflected reliably and quickly, typically within seconds. It also means you should be cautious about building features where two people acting on slightly stale data at the same time could cause a real problem — like both claiming the last seat on a flight — because those scenarios may need a stricter, more expensive consistency guarantee that you'd want to flag as a separate engineering conversation.

A database index is a data structure that helps the database find rows faster, much like an index at the back of a book helps you find topics without reading every page. Instead of scanning an entire table row by row, the database can use an index to jump quickly to the relevant records.

For example, if you often run:

```sql
SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = 'a@example.com';
```

an index on `email` can make that lookup much faster. Common index structures, such as B-trees, keep values organized so searching, sorting, and filtering can be efficient.

However, indexes are not free. They must be kept up to date whenever the table changes. When you insert a new row, the database must not only write the row to the table, but also add corresponding entries to each relevant index. When you update an indexed column, the database may need to remove the old index entry and insert a new one. When you delete a row, it must also remove or mark index entries as deleted.

This extra maintenance takes CPU, memory, and disk I/O. The more indexes a table has, the more work each write operation requires. Indexes also consume storage space and can increase locking or contention under heavy write loads.

So indexes are a tradeoff: they often make reads much faster, especially searches and joins, but they can make inserts, updates, and deletes slower because the database has more structures to maintain.

A database index is a data structure (e.g., B-tree) that speeds up reads by enabling efficient lookups on specific columns without scanning the entire table. It slows writes because every insert, update, or delete must modify both the table and all associated indexes to keep them consistent, adding extra I/O and CPU overhead.

A database index is a specialized data structure, most often a B-tree or hash table, that the database maintains alongside a table’s rows. It stores copies of selected column values together with pointers (or row identifiers) back to the actual data, allowing the engine to locate matching rows without scanning every record.

Because the index is a separate, ordered copy of data, every write must keep it synchronized. An INSERT requires the database to find the correct leaf position in the index and insert a new key-pointer pair; in a B-tree this can trigger node splits and rebalancing. An UPDATE to an indexed column means deleting the old entry and inserting a new one. A DELETE removes the corresponding index entry. Each of these steps adds CPU work, extra random I/O, and lock contention. When several indexes exist on the same table, the cost multiplies because every index must be updated atomically within the same transaction. The net result is that write throughput drops and transaction latency rises, even though read queries become faster.

## Database Indexes

A database index is a separate data structure — commonly a B-tree or hash table — that the database maintains alongside a table. It stores a subset of columns in a pre-sorted, quickly searchable form, along with pointers back to the full rows. This lets the database locate matching rows without scanning every record in the table, dramatically speeding up reads and lookups.

### Why Indexes Slow Down Writes

The performance cost comes from the fact that **the index must stay synchronized with the underlying table at all times**. Every time you insert, update, or delete a row, the database cannot simply modify the table — it must also update every index defined on that table.

This creates several concrete costs:

- **Extra I/O** — the index pages must be read into memory, modified, and written back to disk.
- **Structural rebalancing** — a B-tree index may need to split or merge nodes to maintain its sorted, balanced structure after an insertion.
- **Lock contention** — updating index structures can require additional locks, increasing contention under concurrent workloads.
- **Write amplification** — a single logical write to the table can become multiple physical writes across several index structures.

The more indexes a table has, the heavier each write becomes. This is why database designers treat indexes as a deliberate trade-off: **optimizing for read speed at the cost of write speed**, and only adding them where query patterns justify it.

Adding a message queue decouples the services: producers don’t need the consumer to be immediately available, spikes can be buffered, retries are easier, and failures are isolated. It can improve resilience and scalability. Tradeoffs include higher complexity, extra infrastructure, operational monitoring, possible message loss or duplication, ordering issues, and harder debugging. It also changes semantics: instead of immediate success/failure, you often get eventual consistency and need idempotent consumers.

Putting a message queue between two services changes the interaction from synchronous request/response to asynchronous communication. The main benefit is **decoupling**: the caller no longer needs the callee to be available or fast at the exact moment of the request. This can improve resilience, absorb traffic spikes, and let each service scale independently. Queues also provide buffering, retry mechanisms, and can make workflows more tolerant of temporary failures.

However, the tradeoff is increased **complexity**. Instead of getting an immediate response, the caller must deal with delayed processing and eventual consistency. If the caller needs to know the result immediately, a queue may not fit well or may require additional patterns such as callbacks, polling, correlation IDs, or a separate response queue.

Queues also introduce operational concerns: monitoring queue depth, handling poison messages, configuring retries and dead-letter queues, ensuring message durability, and managing broker availability. Debugging becomes harder because a single logical operation is now split across time and systems.

There are also semantic challenges. Message delivery is often “at least once,” meaning consumers must be idempotent to safely handle duplicate messages. Ordering may not be guaranteed unless explicitly designed for, and even then it can reduce throughput. Schema/version compatibility between producers and consumers must be managed carefully.

The producer can publish messages and continue without waiting, while the consumer processes them independently. It also enables patterns such as retry queues, dead-letter handling, and replay for debugging or recovery.

## Adding a Message Queue Between Services

### What You Gain

**Decoupling and resilience** are the primary benefits. If the downstream service goes down, the upstream service keeps running — messages accumulate in the queue rather than causing cascading failures. This makes the overall system more fault-tolerant.

**Load leveling** lets you absorb traffic spikes. Instead of the downstream service getting hammered during peak load, it processes messages at a sustainable rate. This can eliminate the need to over-provision infrastructure.

**Independent scaling** becomes easier since each service scales based on its own throughput needs rather than being locked to the other's capacity.

### What You Lose

**Synchronous response** is the most significant tradeoff. If the caller needs an immediate result — a payment confirmation, an availability check — async messaging requires awkward workarounds like callback queues or polling, adding complexity that often negates the benefits.

**Simplicity disappears quickly.** You now operate and monitor an additional piece of infrastructure. Debugging failures is harder because the request/response cycle is broken across time. Tracing a transaction end-to-end requires correlation IDs and distributed logging.

**Consistency guarantees weaken.** You trade strong consistency for eventual consistency, which may be unacceptable depending on the domain.

**Message ordering, deduplication, and dead-letter handling** all become your responsibility.

### The Core Question

Ask whether the interaction is genuinely fire-and-forget or event-driven by nature. If the answer is yes, a queue fits naturally. If the caller truly needs a response before proceeding, the synchronous model is probably the right one.

Idempotency means a customer can safely repeat the same action and get the same result, without accidental duplicates. If they click “pay” twice or a network retry happens, they should be charged once, not twice. It does not mean every request succeeds; it means repeated identical requests won’t create extra side effects. Promise safety from duplication, not guaranteed success.

Idempotency means that if the same request is received more than once, the outcome is the same as if it had been received once.

A simple example is an elevator button. Pressing “up” once or five times should not summon five elevators or make the elevator arrive faster. The system recognizes that the desired outcome is already requested: an elevator should come. Extra presses do not create extra effects.

This matters because in real products, duplicate requests happen. A customer may click “Pay” twice, their phone may lose connection and retry, or our servers may not know whether a previous request succeeded. Without idempotency, retrying can create bad outcomes: two charges, two orders, duplicate emails, repeated refunds, or multiple account changes.

For customer promises, idempotency lets us say, “It is safe to retry this action” or “If you do not receive a response, trying again will not duplicate the result.” But it does not automatically mean every action can be undone, nor does it mean nothing can ever go wrong. It means we design the system to recognize repeated attempts for the same intended action and return the same result or current status.

The key product question is: which actions must be safe to repeat? Payments, order creation, refunds, subscription changes, and form submissions often need this. The customer-facing promise should be specific: “You won’t be charged twice for the same checkout attempt,” not a vague promise that “duplicates can’t happen anywhere.”

Idempotency ensures that repeating the same customer action, say submitting a payment after a network glitch, produces the same outcome as doing it once. This lets you promise customers that retries won’t trigger duplicate charges or orders, even when their connection drops, while still acknowledging that rare edge cases may need manual support rather than guaranteeing flawless automation every time.

Idempotency is the property that lets you safely repeat an action without changing the final outcome beyond what happened the first time. Picture a customer tapping “buy” on a checkout screen; the network drops and the app never receives confirmation. If the operation is idempotent, the customer can tap again or the app can retry automatically and the result stays the same: one order placed, one charge made, one confirmation email sent. Without it, the same tap could create duplicate orders or double charges, forcing you to decide whether to promise “we’ll clean it up later” or to tell customers “don’t retry.”  

When you design or sell a feature, ask which customer actions must remain safe to repeat—payments, address updates, subscription cancellations—and which must not—issuing a one-time coupon code or starting a unique workflow. For the repeatable ones you can confidently tell customers they may press the button again if nothing seems to happen, or that the service will retry on their behalf without side effects. That promise reduces support tickets, builds trust during flaky connections, and lets you set clearer expectations about what “success” and “failure” actually mean to the user.

Imagine a light switch that's already on. Flipping it "on" again changes nothing. That's idempotency — doing the same action twice produces the same result as doing it once. For customers, this means you can safely promise that retrying a failed payment, submission, or request won't cause duplicates. It's the difference between "try again" being safe advice versus a dangerous one.

Imagine you're sending a text to a friend asking them to pick up one carton of milk. If the message delivers twice because of a glitch, a good friend understands the intent and still buys just one carton. That's idempotency: doing the same operation multiple times produces the same result as doing it once.

This matters because networks are unreliable. When a customer clicks "Submit Order" and nothing seems to happen, they often click again. Or their app retries automatically in the background. Without idempotency, that double-click becomes two charges, two shipments, two support tickets, and one very angry customer.

When you're deciding what to promise customers, the key question is: what happens if this action runs twice? For anything involving money, inventory, or irreversible consequences, you want your engineering team to guarantee idempotency before you commit to reliability promises in your marketing or contracts. If they can't yet, you need softer language and a clear recovery path.

The honest tradeoff is that building idempotency takes extra engineering effort. It usually means tracking whether a request has already been processed, which adds complexity and cost. So you don't need it everywhere, just on the actions where a duplicate would cause real harm.

Think of it as the difference between a light switch and a doorbell. Pressing a doorbell twice rings twice. Flipping a light switch twice leaves you exactly where you started.
